title: The satisfies Operator
summary: Check that a value fits a type while keeping its more specific inferred details.
nestedConcepts: Check a value against a shape
Choose between precision and a broad type

subtopics.title: Check a value against a shape
subtopics.explanation: The `satisfies` operator checks that an expression fits a required type without replacing the expression’s inferred type. For example, a route map can be checked against `Record<string, RouteConfig>` while retaining its exact route keys. This catches missing or wrongly typed fields at compile time.

subtopics.title: Compare satisfies with an annotation
subtopics.explanation: A type annotation declares the variable as the annotated type, which can widen specific values. `satisfies` checks compatibility while preserving more of the expression’s useful detail. Choose an annotation when you want the variable to be used through the broader declared type.

subtopics.title: Remember satisfies is compile-time only
subtopics.explanation: `satisfies` is removed during compilation and adds no runtime validation. It cannot verify JSON, API responses, or user input. Pair it with runtime validation when data can be incorrect while the program is running.

subtopics.title: Keep configuration values precise
subtopics.explanation: A configuration map can use `satisfies` to check that every entry follows a shared shape while preserving each key and literal value. This helps autocomplete stay specific. For external configuration files, validate the parsed data at runtime as well.

subtopics.title: Choose between precision and a broad type
subtopics.explanation: Use `satisfies` when you need both a shape check and precise inference. Use an explicit annotation when downstream code should depend only on a stable, broader contract. This distinction keeps types helpful without exposing every implementation detail to callers.

foundations.overview: The satisfies operator checks whether an expression matches a type. Unlike an annotation, it usually preserves the expression’s narrower inferred type. This helps validate configuration objects without losing useful literal information.
foundations.mentalModel: It is like checking a packed bag against a list without replacing the bag’s item labels.
foundations.whyItMatters: It catches shape mistakes while keeping precise editor support.

keyTakeaways: A type annotation can widen the variable’s visible type.
satisfies does not change runtime JavaScript.
It is useful for typed configuration maps.
Use it where precise inference matters.

codeLab.title: Check a Configuration Without Widening
codeLab.instructions: Add a satisfies check so every route has a string path and a boolean public flag. Preserve the exact route names.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The type checker accepts safe values and reports mismatches at compile time.
hints: Keep external values typed as unknown until you check them.
Use a type feature that preserves the exact information you need.
